Home.heroHeadline: Cloth dyed in a living vat
Home.heroSub: Cold-fermented, one hundred percent natural indigo — woven and resist-dyed by hand, so no two pieces are alike.
Home.thesisBody: The blue comes from the kram plant — a cold, fermented, wholly natural vat tended by hand. Sakon Nakhon is recognised by the World Crafts Council as a World Craft City for Natural Indigo.
Home.chapterHeadline: Raising an indigo vat is like raising a child
Home.chapterBody: The vat is alive. It is fed, kept warm, and read each morning by its colour and scent. Cloth is folded, bound, and lowered in — then lifted to the air, where it turns from green to deep blue before your eyes.

Story.title: The kram plant, the living vat, the hand
Story.lead: Kram Sakon makes living indigo in Sakon Nakhon — a slow craft of plant, water, time, and the human hand.
Story.s1Body: Indigo begins as a leaf. The kram plant is grown, cut, and steeped until its pigment releases into water — the first step in a process measured in days, not minutes.
Story.s2Body: The dye is a cold, fermented, one-hundred-percent natural vat. It is alive: fed with care, kept at the right warmth, and read each morning. Raising an indigo vat is like raising a child.
Story.s3Body: Cloth is folded and bound — shibori — then dipped and lifted, again and again. With air, the green oxidises into deep blue. Because every fold and every dip is made by hand, every piece is one of a kind.
Story.s4Body: Sakon Nakhon is recognised by the World Crafts Council as a World Craft City for Natural Indigo — a home of this living tradition.
